articles.title: Dutch police arrest 'security pro' in ShinyHunters probe
articles.text: Dutch police have arrested a 24-year-old man on suspicion of involvement with the prolific ShinyHunters cybercrime group. Cops announced the arrest on Monday night and said the Amsterdam resident would appear before judges at Rotterdam District Court today (Tuesday). Officers have not named the suspect. However, a company has identified a person they believe to be the suspect as working for them as an offensive security lead. Dutch broadcaster RTL and other newswires have also published a name. The Register chooses not to do so until a name is officially released by law enforcement. Authorities have not disclosed what conduct he is suspected of or identified any attacks allegedly involving him. The timing has focused attention on the investigation into the February breach of Dutch telco Odido, which was claimed by ShinyHunters and affected 6.2 million customers. Police have not said whether the individual is suspected of participating in that attack or whether he is the caller heard in an audio recording released this month. Investigators said the Odido intrusion began when a Dutch-speaking caller posed as an IT colleague and persuaded a customer service employee to provide access to an internal system. Police released part of the call on September 8 and subsequently received 20 tips, including what they described as "some very interesting information that the investigation team can use moving forward." Reuters reports the suspect was arrested on September 15 and that forensic investigators visited an Amsterdam office to make the arrest that night. They said police deployed flashbang grenades during the operation, although the account does not make clear where they were used. The arrest came a week after the public appeal. The person the news reports named was convicted several years ago of hacking, data theft, and extortion, and sentenced to four years in prison, one year suspended. He subsequently returned to legitimate cybersecurity work. ShinyHunters denial that it is linked to the named individual comes days after it boasted of compromising an FBI recruitment system, exclusively telling The Register that it hacked the FBI to "protect our business." The move is part of an escalating run of attacks and extortion attempts attributed to the group. ® Updated to add at 1425 UTC: Following the 24-year-old's hearing in Rotterdam on Tuesday, Dutch police are still witholding the man's name, despite wider reporting identifying an individual as the alleged suspected hacker. The police also dispelled any suggestion that the suspect they arrested is thought to have been involved in the hack on Dutch telco Odido. Politie's National Investigation and Intervention Unit and its High Tech Crime Team are heading up two separate investigations into the Amsterdam man: One related to his alleged involvement with ShinyHunters and another possible double-murder inquiry. After the man's arrest on September 15, police said on Tuesday that "a large amount of information was found on his laptop, including details about two murders that were to be committed abroad. "There are indications that the suspect gave the order for this." The suspect is being held in "complete isolation" while investigators work through the two separate cases. Stan Duijf, head of operations at Politie's National Investigations and Special Operations, said: "Arresting cybercrime suspects is an important intervention within our broad fight against it. The ShinyHunters group is responsible for a large number of national and international victims. It is good that we have been able to arrest a suspect in the investigation into this group." The FBI has not released an official statement alongside their Dutch counterparts, although director Kash Patel said the feds assisted Dutch investigators and are working to unearth additional leads. The gang claimed to The Reg in a message: "As we said last time the Dutch police are unskilled and incompetent. That individual has no association with us."

articles.title: Redmond to millions of Power BI users: You’re Fabric app devs now
articles.text: Microsoft is pushing its data analytics and engineering environment to a new set of commercial users that are an “order of magnitude” greater than its current base. Power BI has become a popular biz intelligence system - with more than 425,000 customers worldwide - particularly among customers of the Microsoft Dynamics application portfolio. Now, Microsoft execs are trying to exploit this penetration by offering Power BI customers high-end database services and app building tools available on its Fabric data analytics and engineering platform. Customers who license Power BI Pro and Power BI Premium Per User will get Fabric Apps and Fabric Database capabilities (up to 1GB per app), along with security, at no additional cost. Microsoft argues that the Apps customers are building in Fabric can be ported to Power BI without much additional work or cost. Arun Ulag, exec veep at Microsoft, told The Register: “We have 40,000 Fabric customers today. Power BI is an order of magnitude larger, with 425,000 customers: organizations, not individuals. The usage of Power BI exceeds 35 million business users every month,” he said. Microsoft is now offering this user base the ability to build data analytics-style apps using Rayfin, an open source SDK. The company says Rafin will let users create their own data applications that accept inputs, write back data, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows across to Fabric. Each application gets a 1GB Fabric SQL database, authentication, and security. As an application grows, users can expand its functionality and hand it off to developers and IT teams without rebuilding it. By bringing Fabric application development to Power BI, Microsoft is showing that the “distinctions between a dashboard and an app are disappearing,” Ulag said. Rayfin is designed to work with GitHub Copilot; Claude Code or Codex; or any coding agent, letting users instruct a coding agent to build an application and deploy where they specify, in a Fabric environment.The feature is scheduled to be available in preview in the coming weeks. Fabric was anounced by Microsoft in 2023 as an integrated analytics, data warehouse and data lake environment. It has since added data mirroring to allow users to run analytics on data in other environments without pushing SQL queries directly to them. Last year, the vendor added transactional databases to the environment, including its document database Cosmos DB and Fabric SQL relational system. Microsoft says it is now extending its integration with other platforms, including Salesforce application and data systems. It is previewing bidirectional integration with Salesforce Data Cloud 360, making data from the CRM vendor available across the Microsoft system for analytics and AI, including as business context for Fabric data agents, without duplicating that data. Salesforce also has its own data environment and agent-building platform.®
